title: The Long Way Back
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 14 of 40
content:
The road back from the music festival took twice as long because Greg refused to admit the van was lost.

“I’m not lost,” he said for the fourth time.

“You just asked a cow for directions.”

“The cow was near a sign.”

“The cow was eating grass.”

“It had a thoughtful expression.”

I held the paper map on my lap and tried not to laugh. The festival had ended beneath a pink evening sky. Lila had played a brilliant set. Greg had introduced me to old friends, new musicians, and one man who had made a three-hour argument about harmonicas sound like a spiritual experience.

I had danced with Greg in the grass. I had eaten fried dough. I had listened to him play a new song and felt my whole body recognize the moment before the first verse ended.

Now the van's engine made a worrying noise.

“It sounds like a drawer full of rocks,” I said.

“That’s normal.”

“It is not.”

“It’s a vintage sound.”

“The van is trying to die.”

“It has a flair for drama.”

The engine coughed. Greg guided the van onto the shoulder. A sign announced that the nearest town was twelve miles away.

He turned off the ignition.

Silence filled the cabin.

“I’m going to say something,” I began.

“Please don’t say the van is dead.”

“The van is dead.”

Greg rested his forehead against the steering wheel.

“You said it first,” I added.

“I know.”

The sun lowered toward the fields. Cars passed occasionally, their headlights flashing across the windows. Greg opened the hood and stared into the engine compartment with the confidence of a man who had learned just enough about machines to become dangerous.

“Can you fix it?” I asked.

“Maybe.”

“That word is not mechanically reassuring.”

He found a loose belt, a cracked hose, and a tool he swore had not been in the van when they left. Nothing made the engine willing to restart.

“We’ll call for help,” he said.

He tried his phone. No signal.

I tried mine. One bar appeared, then vanished.

The familiar pressure began in my chest.

Greg saw it. “Hey.”

“I’m fine.”

“I didn’t ask.”

I leaned against the van. “We’re stranded.”

“Temporarily.”

“You don’t know that.”

“No. But I know we have water, food, blankets, and two phones that will eventually find civilization.”

“What if they don’t?”

“Then we become legends of the cow road.”

I tried to laugh. It came out wrong.

Greg wiped his hands on a rag and came to stand in front of me. “Do you want a plan?”

“Yes.”

“We wait until the next car passes, then flag it down if it’s safe. If it doesn’t, we walk toward the town while staying on the shoulder. We keep the lights on until the battery says otherwise. We eat the sandwiches before they become science.”

“You have a plan.”

“I have several.”

“Why didn’t you say that?”

“You were looking at the engine like you wanted it to apologize.”

“It should.”

“I agree.”

The next car stopped. The driver called a tow service and offered them a ride to the town. Greg stayed close to me the entire time, his hand resting lightly against my back whenever the road became uneven.

At the small motel, the clerk gave me a room with two beds and a window facing a field. The tow truck would come in the morning.

“We can take the separate beds,” Greg said.

I looked at him. “Do you want to?”

“No.”

“Then don’t.”

He smiled, but the nervousness did not leave his eyes.

The room was clean, plain, and too quiet after the festival. I showered first. When I returned, Greg sat on one bed with a paper cup of motel coffee.

“Your turn,” I said.

“I’m afraid the shower will judge me.”

“The cow already did that.”

He disappeared into the bathroom. The water turned on. I opened the curtains, then closed them when a moth threw itself against the glass.

When Greg came out, his hair was damp and his shirt clung to his shoulders. I looked away too late.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“You’re wet.”

“That sounds like an observation.”

“It is.”

He sat beside me. “Are you okay?”

“I’m tired.”

“That’s true.”

“And embarrassed.”

“Why?”

“Because the van broke down and I immediately panicked.”

“The van broke down. Panicking was a reasonable response.”

“You made a plan.”

“I panicked too. I just did it under the hood.”

I turned toward him. “You did?”

“I have no idea what half those parts do.”

“You looked confident.”

“I had a rag.”

The laughter came easier this time. Greg leaned back against the headboard.

“I used to think I had to be the person who knew what to do,” he said. “Especially when I was younger. If I was funny enough, useful enough, calm enough, maybe nobody would notice I was terrified.”

“I notice.”

“I know.”

“Does that bother you?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you don’t use it against me.”

The words made me look at him.

Greg reached for my hand. “There’s a difference between being seen and being exposed.”

I turned my palm upward. He laced his fingers through mine.

“I want to be seen by you,” he said. “Even when I’m not impressive.”

“You asked a cow for directions.”

“Exactly.”

I kissed him. The motel room softened around the edges. Greg's hand rose to my cheek, then moved to the back of my neck. He held me close, warm and familiar.

The bed creaked when I shifted. Greg pulled back just enough to look at me.

“Still okay?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want—”

“I want you to stop asking questions for thirty seconds.”

He smiled. “I can try.”

“Try now.”

He kissed me again.

The motel room filled with the quiet sounds of affection. We talked until we were too tired to keep our eyes open and fell asleep with the television muttering softly in the background.

In the morning, the tow truck arrived. The van was repaired with a part the mechanic described as “mostly compatible.” Greg paid, thanked him, and promised not to ask livestock for directions again.

On the road home, my hand rested in his.

“The trip was good,” I said.

“Even the breakdown?”

“Especially the breakdown.”

Greg glanced at me. “You’re developing an alarming appreciation for chaos.”

“I’m developing an appreciation for what you do when chaos arrives.”

His thumb brushed over my knuckles.

The van carried me toward Beach City, toward the bakery and the boardwalk and the couch with a blanket waiting on it.

It had broken down on the way there.

It was still carrying me home.

The scenic route passed through a town with a clock tower, three antique shops, and a bakery that advertised pies in the window. Greg pulled over before I could ask.

“This is not our route,” I said.

“The route has become more interesting.”

“The route is a road.”

“Roads have personalities.”

“You and the van are both impossible.”

He bought a pie. The baker asked whether I was newlyweds. Greg choked on a laugh. I answered that I was simply trying to survive a road trip.

“That was a missed opportunity,” Greg said once I was outside.

“For what?”

“A very specific joke.”

“You can tell it to the cow.”

“The cow would understand.”

I ate pie on a bench beneath the clock tower. The town moved around me slowly: a dog pulling at its leash, an old couple arguing about directions, a teenager carrying a stack of books.

“Do you ever think about living somewhere like this?” I asked.

“Sometimes.”

“A small town. A little house. A kitchen that doesn’t move.”

“Sometimes.”

“Would you?”

Greg looked at the pie in his hands. “I could. I’m not sure I would be happy if I did it because someone else thought it would make me easier to love.”

I nodded. “I understand that.”

“I could also keep the van and visit.”

“You’d park it in the driveway.”

“It would be a guest house.”

“It has delusions again.”

“It has aspirations.”

The conversation did not resolve where either of us would live. It made room for the possibility that home could take different shapes over time.

When I reached Beach City that evening, Greg parked outside my apartment instead of his.

“Do you want to come up?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“You sound tired.”

“I’m tired and I want you.”

The directness made me smile.

Inside, I played music quietly and shared the last of the pie. Greg washed the plates while I unpacked the blankets.

“The van survived,” he said.

“Barely.”

“A lot like us.”

I crossed the room and kissed him. “We’re doing better than barely.”

He held me close. “We are.”

The night unfolded with fewer jokes and more honesty. I talked until sleep became unavoidable, then chose each other in the quiet afterward.

In the morning, Greg left a slice of pie beside my coffee and called it a road-trip blessing.

We ate it together.

Slowly.
